newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss say Sweden received Nazi gold. [CORRECTED 14:45 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Swiss say Sweden received Nazi gold. [CORRECTED 14:45 GMT]

text.p: (Corrects title and text to make clear that the Swiss National Bank is not denying that it might have known about the origin of the gold)
Switzerland's central bank said it was unclear whether it knew in 1943 that gold received from the Nazis was looted by the German army from Belgium.
A spokesman for the the Swiss National Bank (SNB) also said it was clear from its files that Sweden had received gold from the Nazis during World War Two, just like Switzerland.
"It is incorrect that Switzerland was the only neutral country to take gold from the German Reichsbank," spokesman Werner Abegg told Reuters.
He added that the SNB's files, based on contacts between Sweden and Switzerland in 1943, clearly showed that Sweden had also received gold from the Reichsbank.
Switzerland had specifically asked Sweden in 1943 whether it was continuing to accept gold from Germany. Sweden had answered that it still accepted gold and did so in 1943 and 1944.

The SNB was reacting to a document released on Thursday by U.S. Senate Banking Committee Chairman Alfonse D'Amato saying the Swiss central bank took in 100 tonnes of gold from the Nazis in 1943 after Sweden refused because the bullion had been stolen by Germany from Belgium.

Abegg said the Allied Forces knew of this document during talks leading to the 1946 Washington Accord. In this accord, signed with Britain, the United States and France, Switzerland agreed to return $60 million worth of the gold it handled for Germany, although the U.S. believed it had about $400 million.
Abegg said it was critical to distinguish between what was known during the war and what came to light after 1945.
Abegg acknowledged that documents showed neutral countries had been warned about the gold, but the full details of the transactions first became clear after the war.
The extent of the central bank's knowledge of the transactions at that time is still being researched.
"It first became known after the war that most of the gold had been melted down," Abegg said.
However, D'Amato, a New York Republican and a severe critic of Swiss actions during and after the war, said a truly neutral country would not have accepted the gold.

The Allies had warned neutral nations in January 1943 not to accept gold stolen from Nazi-occupied countries because the Germans were using it to buy supplies in neutral countries to further their war efforts.

D'Amato's document, a 1946 report by the U.S. political affairs adviser for the American occupation government then ruling Germany, said the Swiss accepted the 100 tonnes of stolen Belgian gold, worth $123 million at the time, after it had been rejected by Sweden.
